title: Edu-Homily Watch: Do Students Need to Like Their Teachers to Learn?
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio interrogates the popular claim -- traceable to Rita Pierson's viral 2013 TED Talk -- that students won't learn from teachers they don't like, arguing it's an appealing but incomplete picture of how learning happens. He acknowledges positive teacher-student relationships correlate with engagement and achievement, citing Roorda et al.'s meta-analysis and Hamre and Pianta's early-years research, but argues instructional quality, not personal rapport, is the dominant driver of learning: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction and Hattie's meta-analyses both identify explicit teaching, guided practice, and formative assessment as more influential than relational factors. Pondiscio cites Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory to argue autonomy and competence can drive motivation independently of relatedness, and points to standardized test-prep programs and asynchronous online learning as environments where minimal personal connection doesn't prevent learning. His central inversion, drawing on Hattie and the Gates Foundation's Measures of Effective Teaching project, is that the causal arrow runs backward from the popular claim: students don't learn from teachers because they like them, they come to like teachers because those teachers help them learn, especially once a 'warm demander' approach earns delayed but durable respect.
points: Pondiscio's central inversion of the popular claim -- 'students learn from teachers they like. But they like teachers they learn from' -- reorders cause and effect in a way that changes what a teacher should actually prioritize.

He backs the instructional-quality argument with two heavyweight citations (Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, Hattie's meta-analyses), both of which identify structural teaching moves, not relational warmth, as the stronger predictor of outcomes.

The Measures of Effective Teaching (Kane et al., 2013) finding he cites is specific: students' positive attitudes toward teachers were most closely tied to perceived ability to manage a classroom and set rigorous, challenging work -- not to personal likability per se.

His 'warm demander' framing explains the apparent contradiction in the data: students may initially resist a demanding teacher, but often come to respect and even like that teacher once they experience real growth.
quotes: Students won't learn from someone they don't like. It's a lovely sentiment: warm, intuitive, and flattering to those of us who spend our days in classrooms.
as appealing as the idea is, it’s simply not true—or at least, it’s an incomplete picture of how learning happens.
The most powerful driver of student learning isn’t personal chemistry with a teacher; it’s the quality of instruction.
The key is the student perception that the teacher is someone who cares for them, and thus high trust is critical," Hattie writes.
Most important are students' perception of a teacher's ability to control a classroom and to challenge students with rigorous work.
students learn from teachers they like. But they like teachers they learn from.
